changes.before: A token was committed before .gitignore was added. Is the token now removed from history?
changes.after: An ignore rule skips matching untracked files. It does not erase files already saved in Git.

before: An ignore rule prevents matching untracked files from being included by ordinary add operations. It does not erase a file already recorded in Git history.
Suppose debug.log is already tracked. Adding debug.log to .gitignore does not make its future edits disappear from status. A file’s tracked status and its ignore match answer different questions.

ls-files lists paths known to the index. A listed debug.log is tracked. status --short summarizes staged and unstaged changes. Inspect both before deciding whether a cleanup is appropriate. Do not use a secret file for this exercise.
Changed situation: A token was committed before .gitignore was added. Is the token now removed from history?
Ignore rules do not rewrite commits. A real exposed credential needs rotation and an appropriate history-remediation process.
after: An untracked file is one Git has not added to its index. .gitignore lists files to skip during ordinary add operations.
If debug.log is already tracked, adding its name to .gitignore does not stop Git from reporting its edits.

Use a harmless practice file to inspect its state.

```bash
git ls-files -- debug.log
git status --short
```
git ls-files lists files in the index. If debug.log appears, it is tracked. git status --short shows a short report of staged and unstaged changes.
Adding an ignore rule does not rewrite past commits. A file saved in an earlier commit remains in that history.
A token is a secret key that can grant access. If a real key was exposed, replace or revoke it and follow the service's recovery steps. An ignore rule alone does not fix the exposure.
